title: Stress
in30Seconds: Stress is the body's response to demands or threats. The triggers — stressors — range from daily hassles to major life events to chronic strain. In a real emergency the alarm is useful: Walter Cannon named it the fight-or-flight response, and Hans Selye mapped its longer course as the general adaptation syndrome. The alarm gets expensive when it keeps ringing: chronic stress wears on the body. Not all stress is bad, though. Selye called the beneficial kind eustress. Stress is the body's alarm system — useful, and costly when overused.
whyItMatters: Stress is not a classroom abstraction; it is the body's oldest alarm system, and everyone lives with it. Academically, the topic connects psychology to biology: fight-or-flight and the general adaptation syndrome are the bridge between what you feel and what your body does. Practically, understanding stress changes how you read your own experience — a racing heart before a presentation runs on the same machinery that once fueled a sprint from a predator, and knowing that makes the feeling less mysterious. It also gives you a steadier frame for health claims: chronic stress is real, and so is the honest point that not all stress is harmful. How people manage stress belongs to the next topic; this lesson is the foundation it builds on.
learningObjectives: Define stress as the body's response to demands or threats, and attribute the working definition to Hans Selye.
Distinguish daily hassles, major life events, and chronic strain as types of stressors, with an original example of each.
Explain the fight-or-flight response, name Walter Cannon as the researcher who identified it, and analyze why the response often mismatches modern life.
Describe the three stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome — alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
Explain, factually, how chronic stress wears on the body, and distinguish eustress from distress with an original example.

collegeVersion.heading: What stress is
collegeVersion.body: The working definition is response-based: stress is the body's reaction to demands or threats. Hans Selye, the endocrinologist who pioneered stress research, defined stress as the response of the body to any demand, whether caused by pleasant or unpleasant conditions (Selye, 1976). The APA Dictionary of Psychology agrees: stress is the physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors, touching nearly every body system. The word response is the heart of it — stress is what the body does about the event, not the event itself. Original example: Maya's phone buzzes with the acceptance email she has awaited for months; her heart pounds — the identical rush she felt last month when a stranger's car slid through the intersection in front of her. Good news and near-miss: one body, same alarm.

collegeVersion.heading: Stressors: what sets off the alarm
collegeVersion.body: A stressor is any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress. Stressors come in three families. Daily hassles are the minor irritations of ordinary life, and they build on one another, leaving people just as stressed as major events (Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer, & Lazarus, 1981). Original example: Priya's bus is late, her coffee lid pops off in her bag, and the office printer jams twice — nothing catastrophic, everything cumulative. Major life events are changes that demand significant readjustment, from moving house to a new job to a divorce (Holmes & Rahe, 1967). Original example: Marta and her partner move to a new city the same month both start new jobs — a chosen move, and still a stretch of stress. Chronic strain is the third family: conditions that persist over an extended period — long-term unemployment, unrelenting caregiving. Original example: Deniz has commuted three hours a day for two years to a warehouse job he cannot afford to leave.

collegeVersion.heading: The stress response: fight-or-flight
collegeVersion.body: Walter Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, first articulated and named the body's immediate reaction to a perceived threat: the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932). Faced with danger, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands flood the body with epinephrine and norepinephrine: the heart speeds up, breathing quickens, pupils dilate, blood flows to the muscles, and digestion slows. The point is energy mobilization — the body prepares to fight or flee. Original example: Nia is crossing the street when a car runs the red light and swerves toward her; within a second her heart pounds and her breath shortens as she jumps back onto the curb. The honest note: this machinery is ancient, tuned for physical emergencies like predators, falls, and fights. Most modern stressors — a deadline, an argument, an inbox — do not call for fighting or fleeing, so the alarm rings with no physical action to follow.

collegeVersion.heading: The general adaptation syndrome: Selye's three stages
collegeVersion.body: Selye asked what happens when stress does not end quickly. His answer, the general adaptation syndrome (GAS), describes three stages of responding to prolonged stress (Selye, 1936; 1976). The alarm reaction is the body's immediate mobilization on facing a threat — roughly the fight-or-flight response. Original example: a lifeguard hears a scream from the pool and is instantly alert, heart racing. The stage of resistance follows if the stressor continues: the initial shock wears off, the body adapts and keeps functioning, yet remains on alert, ready to respond with less intensity. Original example: by the second week of final exams, the first-day panic has faded, but the student sleeps lightly and stays keyed up. Exhaustion arrives if the stressor drags on long enough: adaptation fails, resources are depleted, and the body's resistance breaks down — illness and disease become more likely. Original example: after five months of caring for a sick parent, Rosa feels wrung out, sleeps poorly, and catches every cold that passes through her household.

collegeVersion.heading: Stress and health: when the alarm keeps ringing
collegeVersion.body: The stress response is built for short emergencies, not for years of low-grade ringing. When the reactions that compose it are chronic, or frequently exceed normal ranges, they produce cumulative wear and tear on the body (McEwen, 1998). The mechanisms are concrete: sustained elevated levels of the stress hormone cortisol can weaken immune system functioning, leaving a person more open to infection and disease, and blood pressure that stays high under prolonged strain can take a toll on the heart. Original example: a bakery owner running a six-day-a-week shop for years is winded on the stairs and catches every flu his staff brings in — the bill for an alarm that has not fully stopped ringing since he opened. What people do about chronic stress — coping — is its own topic; this lesson only describes what the alarm does.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: eustress, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Not all stress is bad. Selye pointed out that stress can be a positive, motivating force, and he gave the good kind a name: eustress, from the Greek eu, meaning good (Selye, 1974). The APA Dictionary defines eustress as the positive stress response that comes from challenging but attainable and worthwhile tasks, generating fulfillment and high performance. Original example: a violinist feels a flutter of nerves before her first solo recital and uses the extra energy to play with more focus and finish stronger than in rehearsal. The harmful kind, distress, overwhelms. That leads to the honest framing of this lesson: stress is the body's alarm system. It is useful because it mobilizes you in genuine emergencies, and expensive because every alarm costs something — the bill comes due when it rings too often or too long. Stress is not the enemy. It is a tool with running costs.

vocabulary.definition: The body's physiological and psychological response to demands or threats — the working definition, attributed to Hans Selye, covers any demand, pleasant or unpleasant.
Any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress; stressors include daily hassles, major life events, and chronic strain.
The minor irritations and annoyances of everyday life that build on one another and can leave people just as stressed as major events.
A stressor that persists over an extended period, such as long-term unemployment or unrelenting caregiving demands.
The rapid, whole-body arousal pattern first articulated and named by Walter Cannon, in which the sympathetic nervous system mobilizes the body to fight a threat or flee from it.
Hans Selye's three-stage account of the body's response to prolonged stress: alarm reaction, stage of resistance, and stage of exhaustion.
The beneficial kind of stress, named by Selye, arising from challenging but attainable tasks and associated with fulfillment and high performance.
The harmful kind of stress, in which demands overwhelm the body's ability to adapt and performance, well-being, and health decline.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Stress is the body's alarm system, and the alarm does one job: it tells you something demands your attention. When it sounds, your heart speeds up, your breath quickens, and your muscles tense — that rush is fuel, and it is genuinely useful when the danger is real. The catch is that the alarm was designed for a world of immediate physical dangers: predators, falls, fights. Modern life sets it off with deadlines, arguments, and inboxes — situations where neither fighting nor fleeing helps, so the fuel gets spent on nothing. Ring the alarm constantly and it wears on the body, the way a doorbell that never stops eventually wears on the house. And the alarm is not always bad news: eustress is the good kind, the buzz from challenges you chose, which sharpens you instead of draining you.
eli10.analogy: Think of a smoke detector. A working one sits quietly for years, then screams the instant smoke appears — that is its job, and a screaming detector in a real fire is a lifesaver. Stress is the body's smoke detector: it senses a demand or threat and raises the alarm with a burst of energy and alertness. A home needs its detector; a body needs its alarm.
eli10.analogyLimits: A smoke detector can be silenced with a button or have its battery removed; the body's stress alarm cannot be switched off at will — once a threat is perceived, the response runs on its own. A detector signals one clear danger, while stress responds to anything appraised as demanding, pleasant or unpleasant. And a detector that goes off constantly is merely annoying, while a constantly ringing stress alarm does measurable wear on the body. The detector is also a device you can calibrate; the body's alarm is largely automatic, which is why understanding it matters.

workedExample: Leo, a night-shift nurse, hears a crash from the waiting room at 2 a.m. Instantly his heart pounds and his breath shortens — the fight-or-flight response Walter Cannon described, mobilizing energy before Leo has even decided what to do. The crash was a vending machine tipping over; no one is hurt, and the arousal fades within minutes: an alarm that rang, did its job, and stopped. Leo's other stressor does not stop. For a year, his mother's care has fallen on him, and the demands are unrelenting. Early on, the constant worry kept him wired — an alarm reaction that never quite switched off. Over the months his body adapted, sleeping lightly and staying on edge — Selye's stage of resistance. Lately he wakes exhausted, catches every cold that moves through the ward, and snaps at colleagues; his resources are running down, the stage of exhaustion. The same alarm that saved the vending-machine moment is wearing him out by never fully silencing. The lesson is not that stress is bad. It is that the alarm is useful in emergencies and expensive when it never stops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stress is just a feeling of being overwhelmed or anxious.
commonMistakes.correction: The feeling is only the part you notice. Stress is a whole-body response — physiological and psychological — involving changes in nearly every system of the body, as the APA Dictionary describes.

Selye's definition covers any demand, pleasant or unpleasant. A wedding, a promotion, or a long-awaited move can trigger the same response as a setback — which is exactly why the body, not the event's label, defines stress.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fight-or-flight means you literally fight or run away every time.
commonMistakes.correction: It is the body's arousal pattern — heart, breath, muscles — preparing for physical action. Most modern stressors call for neither fighting nor fleeing, so the response fires with no physical action to match.

commonMistakes.mistake: All stress is harmful and should be avoided.
commonMistakes.correction: Eustress, from challenging but attainable tasks, is beneficial and energizing. The wear-and-tear story belongs to chronic stress — the alarm ringing too often or too long — not to stress itself.

compareContrast.distinction: Both are stress, but eustress comes from challenging yet attainable demands and fuels fulfillment and performance, while distress overwhelms the body's capacity to adapt and drains performance and health.

Acute stressors are brief focal events, like a near-miss on the street; chronic stressors persist over a long period, like a years-long grinding commute, and it is the chronic kind that produces cumulative wear and tear.

compareContrast.b: The alarm reaction of the GAS
compareContrast.distinction: Both describe the body's immediate mobilization in the face of a threat, but fight-or-flight names the sympathetic arousal itself, while the alarm reaction is the opening stage of Selye's longer three-stage sequence of responding to prolonged stress.

keyTakeaway: Stress is the body's alarm system: a useful, whole-body response to demands and threats that becomes expensive when it rings too often or too long — and, as Selye's eustress shows, not every alarm is bad news.

questionBank.prompt: A psychology text says stress is the body's response to any demand, whether pleasant or unpleasant. Which researcher is the source of this working definition?
questionBank.explanation: The response-based definition comes from Hans Selye, the endocrinologist who defined stress as the response of the body to any demand (Selye, 1976), as OpenStax Psychology 2e reports; the APA Dictionary also credits Selye with first describing stress. Walter Cannon named the fight-or-flight response, not the definition of stress itself; Freud and Lazarus are not the source of this definition.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the researcher behind the working definition of stress

questionBank.prompt: Which researcher first articulated and named the fight-or-flight response?
questionBank.explanation: Walter Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, first articulated and named the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932), per OpenStax Psychology 2e, and the APA Dictionary's entry records that it was first described by Cannon. Selye developed the general adaptation syndrome and the eustress concept; Watson is associated with behaviorism and James with early American psychology, and neither named this response.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attribution of the fight-or-flight response

questionBank.prompt: Priya's morning is a string of small frustrations: the bus is late, her coffee lid pops off in her bag, and the office printer jams twice before her first meeting. Which term best describes these stressors?
questionBank.explanation: Daily hassles are the minor irritations and annoyances of ordinary life that build on one another and can leave people just as stressed as major events (Kanner et al., 1981), as OpenStax Psychology 2e describes. A late bus and a jammed printer are irritations, not life changes; nothing here persists over a long period, so chronic strain does not fit; and eustress is beneficial stress, not frustration.
questionBank.skill: Classifying stressors by type in an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Rosa has cared for her sick mother for five months. The first weeks left her wired and sleepless; now the initial shock has faded and she functions — but she stays on edge, sleeps lightly, and feels constantly keyed up. According to Selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage is Rosa in?
questionBank.explanation: The stage of resistance is when the initial shock of the alarm reaction wears off and the body adapts to the stressor while remaining on alert at a reduced intensity (Selye, 1936; 1976) — Rosa's wired-and-sleepless first weeks were the alarm reaction, and her current adapted-but-on-edge state is resistance. Exhaustion is the later stage when adaptation fails and resources are depleted; fight-or-flight is the immediate arousal pattern, not one of the three GAS stages.
questionBank.skill: Applying the stages of the general adaptation syndrome to a scenario

questionBank.prompt: Maya feels a flutter of nerves before her first solo recital, and the extra energy helps her play with more focus and finish stronger than in rehearsal. Which concept best describes her experience?
questionBank.explanation: Eustress is the positive stress response from challenging but attainable and worthwhile tasks, generating fulfillment and high performance; Selye coined the term, and the APA Dictionary defines it that way. Distress is the overwhelming kind of stress, chronic stress persists over time, and the exhaustion stage is the GAS stage of depleted adaptation — none of them fits a nervous-but-focused performance that goes well.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing eustress in an original scenario

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources; all prose is original EliExplains synthesis, no source wording reproduced
provenance.transformation: The working definition of stress was verified against OpenStax Psychology 2e Section 14.1 (read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL) and the APA Dictionary of Psychology entries for stress, stressor, fight-or-flight response, general adaptation syndrome, and eustress (read via the dictionary's public content API). Stressor types and the Holmes-Rahe/Kanner background were verified against Section 14.2; the chronic-stress wear-and-tear facts against Section 14.3. Attribution claims (Selye for the definition, GAS, and eustress; Cannon for fight-or-flight) follow the sources. The mismatch-between-alarm-and-modern-life point is presented as an honest interpretive framing, not a research statistic. All examples, scenarios, and practice questions are original to this lesson.
